headline: Malaysia names Mossad suspects, but no court has convicted one of spying
context: Since 2018, an assassination, an abduction and an armed Israeli's arrest have been linked by officials to foreign intelligence. Every conviction so far is for guns or kidnapping, not espionage.

cards.big: Suspected Israeli operations in Malaysia share a signature: the operative enters on another country's passport.
cards.sub: The 2018 assassins of a Palestinian lecturer used Serbian and Montenegrin papers; the 2024 gunman flew in French. Dubai's 2010 hit squad did the same.

cards.big: Fadi al-Batsh, a lecturer, was shot about 14 times walking to dawn prayers in Kuala Lumpur.
cards.sub: His killers entered on fake Serbia and Montenegro passports and slipped into Thailand after the April 2018 hit. No one has been charged in Malaysia; the deputy PM cited links to a foreign intelligence agency.

cards.big: In 2022, more than a dozen Malaysians abducted a Gaza programmer to force out his phone-hacking software.
cards.sub: Six drew five years' jail in 2025. The alleged ringleader, a private investigator the home minister told Parliament Mossad recruited for RM100,000, still awaits trial.

cards.big: Every conviction so far is for guns or kidnapping, never spying.
cards.sub: Seven years for the Israeli, ten and six strokes for his arms supplier, five each for six abductors. Yet about 50 immigration officers were arrested in 2024 for selling foreigners passage.

cards.big: The danger never lay in a hidden cell. It lies in a border for sale and locals hired at arm's length.
Think of a burglar who never picks a lock.
cards.sub: He pays the doorman, hires local hands who never see his face, and leaves on a passport borrowed from a tourist. The police report says trespassing, not burglary.

cards.big: Ministers now name spies in Parliament, yet the cheapest way in, a bought border and deniable hands, stays open. Suspicion is loud; proof, by design, stays quiet.
